Built on Quality, Trust, and Hard Work
NW General Contractor is the trade name of NW Style Homes 1 LLC, a Washington-registered general contractor (NWSTYSH768DA) based in Everett.

NW General Contractor was founded with a simple idea: homeowners in Snohomish County deserve a contractor they can actually trust. Someone who shows up when they say they will, communicates honestly about costs and timelines, and delivers work they are genuinely proud of.

We are a full-service general contracting company based in Everett, Washington. We handle everything from kitchen and bathroom remodeling to roofing, siding, foundation repair, and complete home renovations. Whether you need a single room updated or your entire home transformed, we manage the project from start to finish so you do not have to.

NW General Contractor started from a real passion for building and a frustration with how the industry often treats homeowners. Too many people in the Everett area have been burned by contractors who overpromise and underdeliver — missed deadlines, surprise costs, poor communication, or work that does not hold up.

We set out to do things differently. Every project begins with a detailed, written estimate. We keep you informed throughout the process, return your calls and messages promptly, and stand behind our work long after the last nail is driven. Our reputation is built one project at a time, and we take that seriously.

As a small, hands-on team, we bring the kind of personal attention that larger companies cannot match. You will not be passed between sales reps and project managers who have never picked up a hammer. The people you meet during your estimate are the same people who will be building your project.
We are a full-service general contractor, which means we handle a wide range of residential construction and remodeling projects:
— Kitchens, bathrooms, flooring, painting, and whole-home renovations. We handle the design coordination, demolition, rough-in, and finish work.
— Roofing, siding, windows, doors, and foundation repair. We protect your home from the Pacific Northwest weather with quality materials and expert installation.
— Decks, patios, pergolas, fencing, outdoor kitchens, and concrete work. We help you make the most of your property year-round.
— Home additions, ADU construction, and detached garages. We manage the full build from permitting through final inspection.
— Built-in shelving, custom trim, wainscoting, mantels, and specialty woodwork that adds character and function to your home.
— Detailed written estimates with itemized costs. No hidden fees, no surprise change orders. If something changes mid-project, we discuss it with you before any additional work happens.

— We source materials from trusted suppliers and choose products rated for Pacific Northwest conditions. From moisture-resistant framing to UV-stable exterior finishes, every selection is made with longevity in mind.

— You will have a dedicated point of contact throughout your project. Regular updates, responsive to calls and texts, and honest about timelines. If something comes up, you will hear about it from us before you have to ask.
— Fully licensed with Washington State, carrying general liability insurance and a surety bond. Your home and your investment are protected.
— We respect your home. Daily cleanup, protective coverings on floors and fixtures, and careful attention to your landscaping and property throughout the project.

We are proud to serve homeowners across Snohomish County, including Everett, Marysville, Lake Stevens, Lynnwood, Mukilteo, Snohomish, Mill Creek, Bothell, and Arlington. As a local company, we understand the unique character of each community — from the historic craftsman homes of downtown Everett to the newer developments in Lake Stevens and the waterfront properties along Mukilteo.

Snohomish County is one of the fastest-growing regions in Washington state, and much of the existing housing stock is 30 to 50 years old or more. Whether you are updating an aging kitchen, replacing a worn-out roof, converting a garage into an ADU, or completely renovating a mid-century home, we have the experience to handle the surprises that come with opening up walls and working on established homes.

We would love to hear about your project. Whether you are in the early planning stages or ready to break ground, contact us for a free, no-obligation estimate. We will visit your home, listen to your ideas, and provide a detailed quote so you know exactly what to expect.

Describe what must change and what should stay

List the rooms or building areas involved, what currently does not work for you, and which existing features you want to preserve. Separate required work from optional upgrades. For example, replacing worn finishes is a different scope from moving a wall, changing plumbing locations, or adding floor area. Photos and rough measurements help explain the question; they do not substitute for an inspection or design.
A mailing address alone does not settle which permitting authority handles a project. Establish whether the property is within a city or unincorporated Snohomish County. The county’s

page provides permit, zoning, and records starting points. Ask the appropriate authority about the proposed work. No general checklist establishes permit requirements or approval for a particular property.

Gather available plans, prior permits, repair records, product selections, and photos of accessible work areas. Mark information that is uncertain. Tell us about access restrictions, occupancy, pets, parking, and spaces that need to remain usable. Do not open walls, disturb suspect materials, or enter unsafe areas simply to prepare an estimate request.
Compare the same scope in each proposal

Ask which demolition, protection, materials, allowances, installation, disposal, and finish work are included. Record exclusions and items requiring another specialist or further investigation. Keep an allowance distinct from a selected product price. A lower total is difficult to compare when the underlying work is different.

Leave the discussion with a named next step: a site visit, a clarified scope, a design decision, or a written proposal. Identify what must be resolved before scheduling. If the scope changes, request a written explanation of the effect on price and timing. Review our
and ask questions before agreeing to work.

Home Remodeling for Arlington's Changing Landscape

Arlington sits at the northern gateway of Snohomish County, a community of approximately 20,000 residents that embodies the transition between the suburban development of the county's southern half and the agricultural and forested landscape that stretches north toward Skagit County and the North Cascades. The Stillaguamish River winds through the valley floor below town, dairy farms still operate on the surrounding flats, and the Cascade foothills rise to the east. Yet Arlington is also a community in transformation, with new subdivisions, expanding retail, and a growing population that has discovered the appeal of small-town living within commuting distance of Everett and the greater Seattle area. NW General Contractor serves Arlington homeowners across this full spectrum, from century-old farmhouses to brand-new construction.

along the Stillaguamish River bottom is Arlington's agricultural heartland, where properties measured in acres rather than square feet define the landscape. The farmhouses that dot the valley range from turn-of-the-century wood-frame structures to mid-century homes built during the region's dairy farming heyday. These properties present renovation challenges that suburban contractors may not be equipped to handle: foundations that have settled unevenly over decades on the valley's alluvial soils, outdated septic systems that must be considered during any expansion, well water systems that affect plumbing decisions, and structures that have been added onto informally over generations without always following building codes.

Homes here were built from the 1920s through the 1960s, ranging from modest bungalows and Cape Cod cottages to larger colonial and ranch-style homes on tree-lined streets. This is classic small-town Washington, with sidewalks, mature elms, and the kind of neighborhood character that attracts buyers looking for something more authentic than a cookie-cutter subdivision.
Remodeling in Haller Park and downtown Arlington focuses on modernizing these well-located homes while respecting their neighborhood context.

These neighborhoods feature homes built from the 2000s through today, with contemporary floor plans, attached garages, and the amenities that new construction provides.

Outside Arlington's city limits, the surrounding rural areas are home to properties on five, ten, or twenty-plus acre parcels. These include working hobby farms, horse properties, and homesteads where families have chosen a more self-sufficient lifestyle. Renovation needs on these properties are often substantial and varied. Older barns may be converted into workshops or living space. Detached structures may need to be brought up to code. Kitchens in older ranch houses may need complete overhauls to serve families who grow and preserve their own food.

County zoning regulations for properties outside city limits may differ from municipal rules, and the larger lot sizes can accommodate more substantial detached living units. We build ADUs on Arlington-area acreages for a variety of purposes: housing for farmworkers or caretakers, independent living spaces for aging parents, and rental units that generate supplemental income for property owners.

Arlington residents enjoy a lifestyle that revolves around the outdoors. The Centennial Trail passes through town, the Stillaguamish River offers fishing and recreation, and the surrounding foothills provide endless hiking opportunities. This outdoor orientation drives demand for covered porches, screened-in patios, and generous decks that serve as three-season living spaces. We design and build outdoor structures that reflect Arlington's rural character, using natural wood, timber-frame construction, and stone elements that complement the surrounding landscape rather than fighting it.

Projects within Arlington city limits go through the City of Arlington's Community Development department, while properties in unincorporated areas fall under Snohomish County's jurisdiction. The two processes differ in timelines, fees, and specific requirements. Building and Remodeling for Lake Stevens Living

Lake Stevens holds the distinction of being the fastest-growing city in Snohomish County, with a population that has nearly doubled in recent years to over 39,000 residents. The city's namesake lake, the largest in the county at over 1,000 acres, sits at the heart of a community that values outdoor recreation, family life, and the kind of natural beauty that draws people away from the urban core. NW General Contractor serves Lake Stevens homeowners with remodeling and construction services designed for the way people actually live here, where the backyard deck matters as much as the kitchen, and where lakefront properties demand a contractor who understands waterfront construction.

Lake Stevens' most distinctive homes are the properties that line the shores of the lake itself. These range from modest cottages built in the 1940s and 1950s as summer getaways to substantial year-round homes constructed more recently. Lakefront remodeling presents unique challenges that require specialized experience. Shoreline setback regulations, critical areas ordinances, and the need to manage stormwater on sloped lots all demand a contractor who has navigated these requirements before.

Composite decking materials are particularly popular here, as they resist the moisture that is inherent to lakeside living and require far less maintenance than traditional wood. Our lakefront deck designs incorporate built-in seating, cable railing systems that preserve sight lines, and integrated lighting for evening use.

Preserving History, Building for Today in Snohomish

The City of Snohomish holds a special place in Snohomish County, not just as the county seat's namesake, but as a community that has consciously preserved its heritage while the region around it has rapidly developed. Known as the "Antique Capital of the Northwest," Snohomish's charming downtown along First Street is lined with Victorian-era commercial buildings housing antique shops, restaurants, and small businesses. The residential neighborhoods surrounding downtown contain some of the finest examples of late 19th and early 20th century architecture in the Pacific Northwest. NW General Contractor brings specialized expertise in historic renovation and thoughtful remodeling to this unique community of approximately 10,000 residents.

The residential streets adjacent to Snohomish's historic downtown are defined by homes built between 1880 and 1920. Queen Anne Victorians with their ornate gingerbread trim, Craftsman bungalows with deep front porches and exposed rafter tails, and Colonial Revival homes with symmetrical facades line avenues shaded by mature trees. These homes represent an irreplaceable architectural legacy, and renovating them demands a contractor who understands the difference between restoring a home and simply updating it.

in Snohomish's historic core prioritizes preservation of character-defining features. Original woodwork, pocket doors, built-in china cabinets, hardwood floors, and decorative plaster details are carefully protected during renovation. Where historic elements have deteriorated, we restore rather than replace, using period-appropriate techniques and materials. At the same time, we modernize the systems that make these homes livable: upgrading knob-and-tube wiring to modern electrical, replacing galvanized plumbing with copper or PEX, adding proper insulation without compromising wall profiles, and installing efficient heating systems that work within the constraints of historic construction.
Kitchen Renovation in Historic Snohomish Homes

The original kitchens in Victorian and Craftsman homes were utilitarian spaces, often small and separate from the rest of the house. Today's homeowners want kitchens that function as the heart of the home, open to dining and living areas, with modern appliances and generous counter space. Achieving this in a historic home requires structural sensitivity, as opening up walls may involve rerouting structural loads, and the kitchen design needs to complement rather than clash with the home's period character.

We design Snohomish kitchen remodels that bridge historical and contemporary aesthetics. Inset cabinetry with period-appropriate hardware, apron-front sinks, and furniture-style islands can create a modern kitchen that looks and feels right in a home built over a century ago. We match trim profiles, respect ceiling heights, and select materials that honor the craftsmanship of the original construction while delivering every modern convenience.

Bathroom remodeling in the Everett area typically costs between $6,000 and $35,000, depending on the scope of work, materials chosen, and the size of your bathroom. Snohomish County labor rates and material costs factor into these numbers. Here's a detailed breakdown to help you plan your budget.
A budget remodel focuses on cosmetic updates that refresh the look without moving plumbing or changing the layout. This includes:
This level works well for rental properties, quick refreshes before selling, or bathrooms that are structurally sound but visually dated.
A mid-range remodel is the most popular option among Everett homeowners. It typically includes:
New tile flooring and shower surround ($2,000-$5,000)
Custom vanity with quartz or granite countertop ($1,500-$3,500)
Tub-to-shower conversion or new shower enclosure ($2,500-$6,000)
New lighting plan with recessed and vanity lights ($500-$1,200)
According to Remodeling Magazine's Cost vs. Value report, a mid-range bathroom remodel recoups approximately 70.1% of its cost at resale — making it one of the best ROI projects you can do.
A high-end remodel transforms your bathroom into a spa-like retreat:
Custom tile work with designer patterns ($4,000-$8,000)
Walk-in shower with frameless glass, rain showerhead, body jets ($5,000-$10,000)
Smart features: heated toilet seat, motion-sensor faucets ($500-$2,000)
Always add a 10-20% contingency for unexpected issues — especially in older Everett homes where hidden water damage or outdated plumbing can be discovered during demolition.
Factors That Affect Cost in the Everett Area
Pre-1978 homes may need lead paint remediation. Homes built in the 1970s-1990s (common in Everett) often have galvanized pipes that should be replaced.
Snohomish County requires permits for plumbing and electrical changes. Budget $200-$500 for permit fees.
Moving plumbing or walls increases cost significantly (add $3,000-$8,000).
Porcelain tile vs. natural stone can swing costs by $2,000-$5,000.
ADA-compliant features (grab bars, curbless shower, wider doorway) add $1,000-$3,000 but increase accessibility and resale value.
Timeline: How Long Does a Bathroom Remodel Take?

Timeline can extend if permits are required, custom materials need to be ordered, or if unexpected issues are found during demolition. The best approach is to have your contractor provide a detailed timeline before work begins.
Tips to Save on Your Bathroom Remodel
— Moving plumbing is the single biggest cost driver. Keeping fixtures in the same locations saves thousands.
— Bathtub refinishing costs $300-$600 vs. $1,500-$4,000 for replacement.
— Modern porcelain tile mimics marble and slate at a fraction of the cost.
— Sometimes new fixtures, paint, and a new vanity are enough to transform the space.
— Always get at least 3 written estimates from licensed contractors.

Yes, if you're changing plumbing or electrical systems. Cosmetic updates (paint, fixtures, vanity swaps) generally don't require permits. Check with the Snohomish County Planning & Development Services office.

Should I remodel my bathroom before selling my home?
Often yes. Updated bathrooms are one of the top features buyers look for. Even a budget refresh ($6,000-$10,000) can make your home more competitive and potentially increase your sale price.

Published July 2026 by NW General Contractor

For homeowners researching decks & patios cost Everett, a practical 2026 planning range is typically $8,000–$50,000, depending on whether the project is a simple patio, new deck, major rebuild, or covered outdoor space. Materials, site access, structural work, finishes, permits, and labor can move an Everett estimate below or above that range.
What a decks & patios costs in Everett

The average cost of a decks & patios in Everett is difficult to reduce to one number because decks and patios are built differently. A deck is an elevated structure that may require footings, framing, stairs, railings, and structural connections. A patio is usually constructed at or near grade using concrete, pavers, gravel, or another hardscape material. Those differences affect labor, materials, permits, and timeline.

For early budgeting, an uncomplicated ground-level patio may typically fall around $8,000–$20,000, while a straightforward new deck may typically cost around $15,000–$40,000. Larger decks, elevated structures, premium decking, extensive stairs, covered areas, or combined deck-and-patio projects may commonly reach approximately $40,000–$100,000, depending on scope. These are planning ranges rather than quotes; site conditions and design decisions can change the actual proposal substantially.

Homeowners comparing decks & patios price per square foot Everett figures should use them cautiously. A basic patio may sometimes budget around $20–$50 per square foot, while a conventionally framed deck may often budget around $45–$100 per square foot. Complex or premium deck construction may fall around $80–$175 per square foot. Small projects can have a higher unit price because mobilization, demolition, permitting, equipment, and finish work are spread across less area.

Everett properties also vary in grade, drainage, access, and existing construction. A flat backyard with direct equipment access is usually easier to price than a sloped or confined site. Before choosing a budget from an online calculator, have the contractor identify what the price includes: demolition, disposal, excavation, footings, framing, surface materials, railings, stairs, drainage work, permits, finishes, and cleanup.

Project scope has the greatest overall influence on cost. Resurfacing a sound deck is a different project from replacing deteriorated framing, and an uncovered patio is different from a roofed outdoor living area. Size matters, but structural height, shape, stairs, guardrails, integrated seating, privacy screens, lighting preparation, and transitions to doors or walkways can matter just as much.

Labor increases when crews must remove old construction, hand-carry materials through narrow side yards, work on a slope, build high above grade, or make careful connections to an existing house. Hidden deterioration can also expand the scope after demolition. A responsible estimate should state how concealed damage will be documented, priced, and approved if it is discovered.

Materials create another large range. Pressure-treated framing and economical surface products generally cost less than premium composite decking, specialty hardwood, metal railing systems, porcelain pavers, or elaborate masonry. Material price alone does not tell the whole story: some products require additional framing, specialized fasteners, more detailed installation, or manufacturer-specific handling.

Finishes affect both appearance and maintenance. Wood decks may need cleaning, staining, or sealing, while concrete patios may include color, texture, scoring, or protective treatment. Paver patios need a properly prepared base and edge restraint. The least expensive finish at installation may not be the least expensive choice over the outdoor space's service life.

Permits and related documentation may be needed depending on the structure, location, height, attachments, electrical work, and other project details. Permit fees and preparation can add roughly $500–$3,000 to some projects, while more involved plans or professional design services may increase that planning allowance to approximately $2,000–$8,000. The applicable requirements should be confirmed for the specific Everett property rather than assumed from a neighboring project.

How to get an accurate estimate

An accurate estimate starts with a defined scope and an on-site review. Measure the approximate area, collect inspiration photos, identify preferred materials, and decide which features are essential. Tell the contractor whether the goal is a new installation, complete replacement, resurfacing, repair, or a coordinated deck-and-patio design. For an existing deck, the contractor should evaluate the visible framing, surface condition, stairs, railings, supports, and connections that can be accessed. Concealed conditions should be identified as an estimate limitation rather than silently assumed.

Ask for a written proposal that distinguishes included work from allowances and exclusions. Smart ways to save without cutting corners

The most reliable savings come from simplifying the design before construction begins. Rectangular layouts, standard material dimensions, direct stair runs, and fewer level changes can reduce labor and waste while still producing a useful outdoor space. Keeping a patio near grade is often less structurally demanding than creating a large elevated deck, although site drainage and access still need proper consideration.

Spend where durability and safety depend on it: preparation, drainage, footings, framing, fastening, flashing, and suitable materials. Decorative upgrades are easier to defer than structural corrections. If the budget is tight, ask the contractor to separate core construction from optional items such as elaborate patterns, premium railings, built-in seating, privacy features, or a future cover.

Compare lifecycle needs as well as installation price. A lower-cost wood surface may fit the initial budget but can involve recurring cleaning and refinishing. A higher-priced composite option may reduce some maintenance, but product lines and installation requirements vary. Request at least two material packages priced for the same layout so the comparison remains meaningful.

Planning early can also limit expensive changes. Finalize dimensions, door transitions, stair locations, furniture zones, and finish selections before ordering materials. If a future hot tub, cover, outdoor kitchen, or other heavy feature is being considered, disclose it during design so the structure and utilities can be evaluated for that intended use.

Finally, keep a contingency rather than using the entire budget on visible finishes. For renovation work, a contingency of roughly 10%–20% of the estimated project range may be prudent, depending on how much existing construction is concealed. Everything you need to know to hire a trustworthy contractor for your home improvement project
Published February 2026 | By NW General Contractor

Hiring a general contractor is one of the most important decisions you'll make during any home improvement project. The right contractor delivers quality work on time and on budget. The wrong one can cost you thousands in delays, poor workmanship, and stress. In the Everett area, where home values continue to climb and the construction market is competitive, knowing how to vet a contractor properly is essential.
This guide walks you through every step of the process, from verifying licenses to spotting red flags, so you can make a confident decision.
This is the single most important step, and it takes about 30 seconds.
Every general contractor in Washington state must be registered with the Department of Labor & Industries (L&I).
Operating without registration is illegal, and hiring an unregistered contractor strips you of most legal protections if something goes wrong.
Enter the contractor's business name or UBI (Unified Business Identifier) number
Review their registration status, specialty, and any infractions
The L&I lookup will show you:
Whether the registration is active and current
The contractor's specialty (general, electrical, plumbing, etc.)
Any complaints, violations, or infractions on file
If a contractor can't provide a registration number or doesn't appear in the L&I database, stop the conversation there. No exceptions.
2. Confirm the $30,000 Surety Bond and Liability Insurance
Washington state requires all registered contractors to carry a
. This bond protects you, the homeowner, if the contractor:
Fails to complete the work as agreed
Doesn't pay subcontractors or material suppliers (who could then lien your property)
In addition to the bond, a reputable contractor should carry
for their employees. Ask for a Certificate of Insurance (COI) and verify it's current. If a contractor's worker is injured on your property and they don't have workers' comp, you could be liable.
Both the bond and insurance status are verifiable through the L&I website. If anything has lapsed, that's a red flag.
Online reviews provide insight into a contractor's reliability, quality of work, communication style, and how they handle problems. Check multiple platforms for a well-rounded picture:

The most widely used review platform. Look at both the overall rating and read individual reviews, especially recent ones. Pay attention to how the contractor responds to negative reviews — professionalism matters.
Tends to have more detailed reviews. Filter for "Contractors" in the Everett area.
Check for the contractor's BBB rating and any filed complaints. An "A+" rating with zero complaints is ideal, but also look at how complaints were resolved.
Community recommendations from your actual neighbors carry significant weight.
What to look for in reviews:
Consistency of positive feedback across platforms
Specific mentions of completed projects similar to yours
How the contractor handled unexpected issues or change orders
Whether projects were completed on time and on budget
Be cautious of contractors with no online presence at all. In 2026, a legitimate, established contractor should have reviews.

Getting multiple estimates isn't just about finding the lowest price — it's about understanding the range of approaches and costs for your project. Three estimates is the minimum; the more complex your project, the more valuable additional perspectives become.
What a Good Estimate Should Include
Specific descriptions of what will be done, not vague summaries
Brands, models, quantities, and quality levels for all major materials
Broken out separately from materials where possible
Start date, milestones, and expected completion date
When payments are due and what triggers each payment
What's covered and for how long
How additional work or changes will be priced and approved
If an estimate is just a single number on a piece of paper, that's not a real estimate — it's a guess. Detailed estimates protect both you and the contractor by setting clear expectations.
Be wary of the lowest bid.

If one estimate is significantly lower than the others (25%+ below the average), there's usually a reason: they're cutting corners on materials, underestimating the scope, using unlicensed subcontractors, or planning to hit you with change orders later.
5. Ask for References and Recent Project Photos
Any contractor worth hiring should be proud to share their work. Ask for:
(within the last 12 months). Actually call them. Ask about the quality of work, communication, timeline accuracy, and whether they'd hire the contractor again.
similar to what you're planning. A kitchen remodeler should be able to show you finished kitchens. An ADU builder should have ADU photos.
An active project you can visit
(with the homeowner's permission). Seeing a jobsite in progress tells you a lot about how a contractor operates — cleanliness, organization, crew professionalism, and quality of in-progress work.
Was the project completed on time and on budget?
How did the contractor handle unexpected issues?
Was communication consistent throughout the project?
Were there any surprises with the final cost?
Would you hire this contractor again?
A solid contract protects everyone. Before signing, make sure the contract clearly addresses these elements:
Everything that will be done, described in detail. If it's not in the contract, don't assume it's included.
Start date, completion date, and consequences for significant delays (excluding weather and material delays beyond the contractor's control).

Tied to milestones, not arbitrary dates. A typical schedule might be 10% deposit, 30% at demolition completion, 30% at rough-in completion, and 30% at final completion. Never pay more than 10-15% upfront.
How changes to the scope will be documented, priced, and approved. Every change should be in writing before work begins.
Exact products, not "or equivalent." If specific materials are important to you, they need to be in the contract.

What the contractor warrants, for how long, and how warranty claims are handled. Washington state provides a 6-year statute of repose for construction defects, but contractor warranties often cover workmanship for 1-2 years.
How disagreements will be handled (mediation, arbitration, etc.).
Who pulls the permits and pays for them. This should be the contractor.

Take the time to read the contract thoroughly. Ask questions about anything you don't understand. A good contractor welcomes questions about their contract — they want you to feel comfortable and informed.
After years in the industry, these are the warning signs that should make you walk away:
Illegal in Washington state. Full stop.
Legitimate contractors accept checks and often credit cards. Cash-only requests are a tax evasion signal and leave you with no payment trail.
A handshake deal offers you zero legal protection.
No legitimate contractor asks for more than 10-15% as a deposit. Demanding full payment before work begins is a classic scam.
"This price is only good today" is a high-pressure sales tactic. A fair estimate should be valid for at least 30 days.
A P.O. Box only or no address at all makes it difficult to pursue the contractor if problems arise.
Every established contractor has satisfied customers. If they won't share references, there's a reason.
A legitimate contractor can produce a Certificate of Insurance within 24 hours.
Storm chasers who show up uninvited after weather events are notorious for poor work and insurance fraud.
An estimate that's 30-40% below others is likely missing something or setting you up for change orders.
8. Questions to Ask During the Estimate Visit
When a contractor comes to your home for an estimate, use the visit to evaluate both their expertise and professionalism. Good questions to ask:
How long have you been in business, and how long have you worked in the Everett/Snohomish County area?
Who will be the day-to-day project manager on my job?
Do you use your own crew or subcontractors? Are the subcontractors also licensed and insured?
How do you handle communication and updates during the project?
What's your approach to keeping the worksite clean and respecting my home?
Have you done projects similar to mine? Can you show me examples?
How do you handle issues that come up mid-project?
What's your current workload and when could you start?
What warranties do you offer on your work?

Pay attention to how the contractor conducts the estimate visit. Do they arrive on time? Do they take measurements and notes? Do they ask you questions about your goals and preferences? A contractor who's thorough during the estimate is likely to be thorough during the project.
When choosing a contractor in Everett, there are real advantages to working with a local company:

Everett, Snohomish County, and other local jurisdictions each have their own permitting processes and code interpretations. A local contractor knows these systems and has working relationships with building departments.
Local contractors have vetted teams of plumbers, electricians, and other specialists who know the area and deliver consistent quality.
A local contractor lives and works in your community. Their reputation is their livelihood. They can't just move on to the next city if a project goes sideways.
Local contractors know the best suppliers in the area and can often get better pricing and faster delivery on materials.
If something needs attention after the project is complete, a local contractor can respond quickly. A contractor based two hours away is far less likely to make a timely warranty visit.
When you hire local, your money stays in the local economy. You're supporting your neighbors and community.
How do I verify a contractor's license in Washington state?
Visit the Washington Department of Labor & Industries contractor verification page at

. Enter the contractor's name or license number to check their registration status, bond information, insurance coverage, and any complaints or violations on file. This free lookup takes about 30 seconds and should be the first thing you do.
How many estimates should I get for a home remodel?

We recommend getting at least three written estimates from different licensed contractors. This gives you a range of pricing, allows you to compare approaches, and helps you identify outliers — both suspiciously high and suspiciously low. Make sure each contractor is bidding on the same scope of work for an accurate comparison.
What are red flags when hiring a contractor?

Major red flags include: no state contractor registration, requesting cash-only payment, no written contract, demanding full payment upfront, pressure to sign immediately, no physical business address, unwillingness to provide references, and being unable to show proof of insurance. Any of these should be a dealbreaker — even if the price is attractive.
What should a contractor's estimate include?

A detailed estimate should include: a complete scope of work with specific descriptions, material specifications and quantities, labor costs, permit fees, a project timeline with milestones, payment schedule tied to completed work, warranty information, and a clear change order process. Vague estimates with a single lump-sum number are a warning sign.
Do contractors in Washington need a bond?

Yes. Washington state requires all registered contractors to carry a $30,000 surety bond. Complete pricing guide with material comparisons for homeowners in Everett, Marysville, Lake Stevens, and surrounding areas
Published April 2026 | By NW General Contractor
What Does a New Roof Actually Cost in 2026?

If you're a homeowner in Snohomish County looking at a roof replacement, you've probably seen wildly different numbers online. That's because roofing costs depend heavily on material choice, roof size and complexity, and local labor rates — and most national guides don't reflect Pacific Northwest pricing.
Here's the reality for 2026: an average roof replacement in Snohomish County costs
on a typical 2,500-square-foot home. Budget options like 3-tab shingles can come in around $16,000, while premium materials like cedar shake or tile can push well past $60,000.

The Pacific Northwest's relentless rain, moss growth, and temperature swings make material choice more critical here than almost anywhere else in the country. A roof that lasts 30 years in Arizona might only last 20 in Everett. This guide breaks down real 2026 pricing for every major roofing material, explains Snohomish County permit requirements, and helps you decide which option gives you the best return on your investment.
Roofing Cost by Material (2026 Snohomish County Pricing)
The table below shows installed costs for a typical 2,500-square-foot roof in Snohomish County, including tear-off of one existing layer, materials, labor, and disposal.

Note: These prices include tear-off, disposal, underlayment, flashing, and standard labor. Complex roofs with steep pitches, multiple valleys, or difficult access will cost more. All pricing reflects Snohomish County labor rates as of early 2026.
Asphalt vs. Metal: Which Is Better for Washington Rain?
This is the most common question we hear from Snohomish County homeowners, and the answer depends on your budget and how long you plan to stay in your home.

If you're staying in your home for 15+ years, metal roofing's long-term ROI often wins in the Pacific Northwest. You'll avoid one or two full asphalt replacements over the same period, and you'll spend almost nothing on maintenance. But if budget is tight or you're planning to sell within 10 years, architectural asphalt shingles deliver excellent performance at a fraction of the cost. Both are solid choices — there's no wrong answer here.
Cedar Shake: The Classic PNW Choice

There's nothing quite like a cedar shake roof on a Pacific Northwest home. The warm, natural look blends perfectly with the evergreen landscape, and it's a material with deep roots in the region's building tradition. Cedar shake remains a popular choice in upscale neighborhoods throughout Snohomish County, particularly in Mukilteo, Mill Creek, and the rural areas around Snohomish and Lake Stevens.
But beauty comes with responsibility. Here's what to know before choosing cedar:

Washington state building codes require cedar shakes to be fire-retardant treated. Class B or Class C fire ratings are the minimum, and some jurisdictions within Snohomish County may have additional requirements, especially in wildland-urban interface zones near Arlington and eastern parts of the county.

Snohomish County's wet climate is paradise for moss and lichen. Cedar roofs need regular treatment with zinc or copper strips and professional cleaning every 2 - 3 years to prevent moisture retention and premature rot.
Individual shakes can split, curl, or deteriorate. Annual inspections catch small problems before they become expensive leaks.
A well-maintained cedar shake roof can last 30 - 40 years, but a neglected one may fail in 15 - 20. Maintenance is not optional with this material.
At $50,000 - $75,000 installed for a 2,500 sq ft roof, cedar shake is a premium investment. Factor in ongoing maintenance costs of $500 - $1,500 per year.

Cedar shake is a beautiful, authentic choice — but only if you're committed to the maintenance. If you love the look but want less upkeep, consider composite shake products or metal shingles designed to mimic cedar's appearance.
What Affects Roofing Cost in Snohomish County
The material cost table above gives you a baseline, but your actual price depends on several factors specific to your home:
Steeper roofs (8/12 pitch and above) require special safety equipment and take longer to install. Expect a 15 - 25% premium for steep-slope work.

Valleys, dormers, skylights, chimneys, and multiple roof planes all add labor time and material waste. A simple gable roof costs significantly less per square foot than a complex hip roof with multiple penetrations.

Until the old roofing comes off, it's impossible to know the full condition of the roof deck. Rot, mold, and water damage are common in Snohomish County homes, especially those with poor ventilation or deferred maintenance.
If the plywood or OSB sheathing underneath is damaged, it must be replaced before new roofing goes on. This adds
depending on how much needs replacing. Partial replacement is common; full replacement is less so but not unusual on older homes.
Tearing off two layers of old shingles costs more in labor and disposal than removing one. Washington allows a maximum of two layers of asphalt shingles.

Homes on hillsides, with limited driveway access, or surrounded by landscaping that needs protection will have higher labor costs. Many homes in the hills around Mukilteo and Lake Stevens face accessibility challenges.

Summer (June through September) is peak roofing season in the PNW. Scheduling in late fall or early spring — when roofers have more availability between rain events — can sometimes mean better pricing and faster scheduling.
A reputable contractor will include a contingency for potential hidden issues, but it's important to understand what might increase your final bill beyond the initial estimate:
Rot and water damage under shingles.
This is the big one. Damaged fascia boards, rafter tails, or decking can add
to your project. Homes built before 1990 or those with a history of deferred maintenance are most at risk. Your contractor should walk you through what they find once the old roof is removed.

Proper attic ventilation is critical for roof longevity in the PNW. If your current ventilation doesn't meet code or isn't adequate for your new roof system, ridge vents, soffit vents, or attic baffles may need to be added. Budget $500 - $2,500.

If your gutters are at the end of their life, it makes sense to replace them during a roof project rather than paying for separate scaffolding and labor later. New gutters run $1,500 - $4,000 for a typical home.

Step flashing, valley flashing, and pipe boot flashing should almost always be replaced during a re-roof. Most contractors include standard flashing in their bid, but custom metalwork around chimneys or complex wall intersections can add $500 - $2,000.

Current building codes may require ice and water shield membrane in valleys and at eaves, improved ventilation ratios, or upgraded underlayment that wasn't required when your roof was last done. These aren't optional — they're code.
Do You Need a Permit to Replace Your Roof in Snohomish County?
This is one of the most misunderstood aspects of roofing in Snohomish County. The rules are actually straightforward once you know them:
Re-roof overlay with the same material type, as long as total layers don't exceed two
Tear-off and replacement with the same material type, as long as roof sheathing is NOT being replaced
Changing roofing material type (e.g., asphalt to metal, or asphalt to cedar shake)
Making any structural changes (adding skylights, modifying roof framing, changing roof pitch)
When a permit is needed, applications can be submitted through
Snohomish County Planning and Development Services (PDS)
. Permit fees typically range from $150 - $500 depending on project scope. Your contractor should handle the permit process for you — if they suggest skipping a required permit, that's a red flag.

For cities within Snohomish County (Everett, Marysville, Lake Stevens, Lynnwood, Mukilteo, etc.), check with the individual city's building department, as some have additional requirements beyond county code.
How Long Does a Roof Replacement Take?
Homeowners are often surprised by how quickly the actual installation goes — and how much time the rest of the process takes:
1 - 3 days of active work for a standard-sized home. Complex roofs or homes requiring extensive deck repair may take 4 - 5 days.
3 - 5 days of active work. Standing seam panels require more precise installation and take longer than shingles.
4 - 7 days. Each shake is hand-placed, making this the most labor-intensive option.

Plan for 2 - 3 weeks from initial consultation to completion. This includes the inspection, estimate, material ordering (some materials have 1 - 2 week lead times), scheduling the crew, and the actual work.
Weather delays are a fact of life in the PNW.

Roofers cannot safely work in rain — the surface is too slippery, and wet conditions compromise adhesive products like roofing cement and ice and water shield. A project scheduled for Monday might not start until Wednesday if rain moves through. Good contractors watch weather windows carefully and will protect any exposed areas with tarps if work needs to pause mid-project. Summer projects have the most predictable timelines; winter and spring projects should build in extra buffer time.
Signs You Need a New Roof
Not sure if it's time? Here are the warning signs Snohomish County homeowners should watch for:

Asphalt shingles shed granules as they age. A few granules are normal, but heavy accumulation — especially dark, gritty sediment — means the shingles are nearing end of life.
Go into your attic on a sunny day. If you can see pinpoints of light through the roof deck, water is getting in (or will be soon).

If you have asphalt shingles installed 20 or more years ago, it's time for a professional inspection even if nothing looks wrong from the ground. Many issues aren't visible without getting on the roof.
Any visible sagging in the roofline indicates structural problems — possibly compromised decking or rafters. This requires immediate attention.

A failing roof often means failing insulation and ventilation. If your heating costs have crept up without another explanation, poor roof performance could be the culprit.
Brown spots on ceilings or walls, peeling paint, or musty odors in the attic all point to active leaks. Don't wait — water damage compounds quickly.

A new roof in Snohomish County costs $18,000 - $30,000 for architectural asphalt shingles and $40,000 - $60,000 for standing seam metal on an average 2,500 sq ft home. Budget 3-tab asphalt starts around $16,000, while premium materials like cedar shake ($50,000 - $75,000) and tile ($45,000 - $100,000) cost significantly more. Final pricing depends on roof complexity, pitch, hidden damage, and accessibility.
Do I need a permit to replace my roof in Snohomish County?

A re-roof overlay with the same material (2 layers or fewer) or a tear-off and replacement with the same material where sheathing is not replaced does NOT require a permit. A permit IS required when changing material type, replacing roof sheathing, or making structural changes. Apply through mybuildingpermit.com or Snohomish County PDS.
How long does a roof replacement take in the Pacific Northwest?

Asphalt shingle roofs take 1 - 3 days of active work, while metal roofs take 3 - 5 days. The total project timeline is typically 2 - 3 weeks including consultation, material ordering, and scheduling. Weather delays are common in the PNW since roofers cannot work safely in rain.
What is the best roofing material for Washington state rain?

Standing seam metal roofing is the best performer in Washington's rainy climate. It sheds water instantly, resists moss growth, handles heavy rain without degradation, and lasts 50 - 70+ years. Architectural asphalt shingles are the best value option and still perform well with proper ventilation and maintenance.
How often should you replace your roof in the Pacific Northwest?

In the PNW, 3-tab asphalt shingles last 15 - 25 years, architectural shingles last 25 - 40 years, and metal roofs last 40 - 70+ years. The wet climate, moss growth, and temperature swings can shorten lifespan compared to drier regions. Annual inspections help catch problems early and extend your roof's life.

text_segments: From quick updates to complete gut renovations, we build bathrooms that combine style, function, and lasting quality.
Professional Bathroom Remodeling Throughout Snohomish County

A bathroom remodel is one of the smartest investments you can make in your home. Whether it is the primary bathroom that needs a complete overhaul or a guest bath that has not been updated in decades, a well-executed renovation improves your daily routine, increases your home's value, and eliminates the problems that come with aging fixtures and outdated plumbing.

NW General Contractor provides full-service bathroom remodeling for homeowners in Everett, Marysville, Lake Stevens, Lynnwood, and communities across Snohomish County. We handle everything from initial design through final walkthrough, including plumbing, electrical, tile work, and finish carpentry.
We offer a complete range of bathroom renovation services, tailored to your needs and budget:

— Floor-to-ceiling tile in showers, accent walls, floor tile, and niche installations. We work with porcelain, ceramic, natural stone, and glass mosaic tiles in patterns ranging from classic subway to large-format modern.
— Single and double vanities in floating, freestanding, and built-in configurations. We source from top manufacturers and also build custom vanities to fit non-standard spaces.

— Frameless glass enclosures, curbless entry for accessibility, bench seating, multiple shower heads, and custom tile work. Walk-in showers are the most requested upgrade in bathroom remodeling today.
— Replacing an underused bathtub with a spacious walk-in shower. This is especially popular in primary bathrooms where homeowners want more functional shower space.
— For bathrooms with enough space, a freestanding soaker tub creates a focal point and adds a luxury feel. We handle the plumbing relocation and floor reinforcement needed for proper installation.
— Electric radiant heating mats installed beneath tile flooring. This is a highly popular upgrade in the Pacific Northwest, where cold mornings are common for much of the year.
— Vanity sconces, recessed ceiling lights, shower niche lighting, and dimmable fixtures. Proper bathroom lighting eliminates shadows at the mirror and creates a comfortable atmosphere.
— New supply lines, drain relocations, water heater connections, and fixture installations. We bring older plumbing up to current code and ensure reliable performance.
— Properly sized exhaust fans with humidity sensors to prevent mold and moisture damage. Many older Everett homes have undersized or poorly vented bathroom fans.
The cost of a bathroom remodel depends on the size of the space, the scope of work, and your material choices. Here are the typical ranges we see for projects in Snohomish County:
($6,000 – $12,000): New vanity, faucet, toilet, mirror, lighting, and fresh paint. Existing tile and layout stay in place.
($12,000 – $22,000): New tile floors and shower surround, updated vanity and countertop, new fixtures, improved lighting, and ventilation upgrade.
($22,000 – $35,000+): Complete gut renovation with layout changes, custom tile work, walk-in shower with frameless glass, heated floors, freestanding tub, and premium fixtures.

A mid-range bathroom remodel recoups approximately 70.1% of the investment at resale. Beyond the financial return, an updated bathroom removes daily frustrations and can be one of the most satisfying home improvements you make.
Walk-In Showers: The Most Popular Bathroom Upgrade
Walk-in showers have become the centerpiece of modern bathroom design. They offer several advantages over traditional tub-shower combos:
— Without a tub taking up floor area, the shower enclosure can be larger and more comfortable.
— Curbless or low-curb entry makes the shower accessible for all ages and mobility levels. This is an important consideration for aging-in-place planning.
— Frameless glass and large-format tile panels mean fewer grout lines and no shower curtain to deal with.
— A well-designed walk-in shower with frameless glass creates an open, spa-like feel that transforms the entire bathroom.

We build walk-in showers with proper waterproofing systems, including Schluter KERDI membrane and Laticrete Hydro Ban, to ensure long-term performance. Proper waterproofing is the most critical component of any shower installation and the area where cutting corners leads to the most expensive failures.

Many homes in Snohomish County were built with bathtub-shower combinations in the primary bathroom. If you rarely use the tub and would prefer a larger, more functional shower, a tub-to-shower conversion is a straightforward project that makes a significant difference in daily use.

The process involves removing the existing tub, reconfiguring the drain and supply plumbing, building a new shower pan (either tiled or pre-formed), installing tile or wall panels, and adding a glass enclosure. Most tub-to-shower conversions can be completed in 7 to 10 working days.

One important note: we recommend keeping at least one bathtub in the home. If you have a two-bathroom home, converting the primary bath to a walk-in shower while keeping the tub in the guest bath is the ideal configuration for both daily use and future resale.

Radiant heated floors are one of the most requested upgrades among our Everett clients. Electric radiant mats are installed directly beneath the tile floor during the remodeling process, adding minimal height to the floor assembly.

The system is controlled by a programmable thermostat, so you can set it to warm the floor before you wake up in the morning. Operating costs are modest, typically $10 to $20 per month for a standard bathroom, depending on usage and electricity rates. The comfort factor is significant, especially during the cool, damp months that define the Pacific Northwest climate from October through May.

Should I convert my tub to a walk-in shower?

Permits are required when the work involves plumbing changes, electrical modifications, or structural alterations. Cosmetic updates like replacing a vanity, painting, or swapping fixtures typically do not require permits. We handle all permit applications and inspections as part of our service.
Are heated bathroom floors worth the investment?

Radiant heated floors are a popular upgrade in the Pacific Northwest, where mornings can be cold and damp for much of the year. text_segments: Custom Carpentry & Finish Work in Everett, WA
Handcrafted built-ins, millwork, and architectural details that elevate your home from ordinary to exceptional.
The Details That Make a Home Feel Finished

Custom carpentry is what separates a house from a home. It is the crown molding that draws the eye upward, the built-in bookshelves that turn a blank wall into a library, the wainscoting that adds depth and character to a hallway, and the custom mantel that becomes the focal point of the living room. These are the details that production builders skip and that homeowners notice every single day.

NW General Contractor provides custom carpentry and finish work for homeowners throughout Everett and Snohomish County. Whether you are adding architectural details to a new construction home, restoring the character of a craftsman bungalow, or completing a remodel with high-quality trim and built-ins, our carpenters deliver precise, lasting work that transforms the feel of your interior spaces.

Built-in shelving transforms unused wall space into functional storage and display areas. Unlike freestanding bookcases, built-ins are integrated into the wall, creating a seamless, architectural look that adds both character and value to your home.

We design and build built-in bookshelves, entertainment centers, window seats with storage, mudroom cubbies, and home office cabinetry. Each unit is custom-sized to fit your space exactly, with adjustable shelves, cabinet doors where you want them, and interior lighting options. We build in paint-grade materials (poplar, MDF) for painted finishes, or in stain-grade hardwoods (alder, maple, oak, walnut) when you want the warmth of natural wood.

Crown molding is one of the most cost-effective ways to add a finished, high-end feel to any room. It bridges the transition between walls and ceilings, creating a visual frame that makes rooms feel more refined and intentionally designed.

We install crown molding in a range of profiles and sizes, from subtle 3-inch cove molding to elaborate multi-piece build-ups that combine multiple profiles for a dramatic effect. Profile options include traditional ogee, colonial, dentil, egg-and-dart, and clean contemporary lines. For rooms with standard 8-foot ceilings, we typically recommend 3.5 to 5.25-inch profiles. Rooms with 9-foot or taller ceilings can support larger, more detailed profiles that match the scale of the space.

Precise miters and coping at inside corners are essential for a professional result. Our carpenters have the experience and tools to handle the irregular corners and out-of-plumb walls that are common in both older and newer homes in Snohomish County.

Wainscoting adds texture, depth, and visual interest to walls, and it serves the practical purpose of protecting lower wall surfaces from scuffs and damage in high-traffic areas. We install several styles of wainscoting:
— Traditional raised panels framed by stiles and rails. This is the classic wainscoting style found in formal dining rooms, entryways, and hallways.
— A more contemporary take on traditional wainscoting, with flat panels set into the frame. Clean and versatile.
— Narrow vertical planks with a distinctive bead groove between each board. Common in cottage, farmhouse, and coastal styles. Works well in bathrooms, laundry rooms, and kitchens.
— Vertical battens applied over flat boards, creating a simple, rhythmic pattern. Popular in modern farmhouse and transitional interiors.
— Horizontal boards with a subtle overlap or gap between them. A versatile option that works on accent walls, fireplace surrounds, and full-room applications.

Standard wainscoting height is one-third of the wall (32 to 36 inches), but we adjust the height to suit the proportions of your room. In rooms with tall ceilings, taller wainscoting (48 to 60 inches) can create a more dramatic effect.

A custom closet system maximizes every inch of storage space and makes your morning routine more efficient. Unlike wire shelving or modular kits, our custom closets are built to the exact dimensions of your space and designed around your specific wardrobe and storage needs.
Double-hang rods for shirts and folded pants
Long-hang sections for dresses and coats
Adjustable shelving for shoes, bags, and accessories

We build closet systems in melamine, paint-grade wood, or stain-grade hardwood, depending on your preferences and budget. Walk-in closets, reach-in closets, linen closets, and pantry organizers are all within our scope.
The fireplace is often the focal point of the living room, and the mantel and surround define its character. We build custom mantels in a range of styles:
— Pilasters, a decorative frieze, and a mantel shelf with crown molding. Built from poplar (painted) or hardwood (stained).
— Clean lines, natural wood, and simple brackets. Quarter-sawn white oak or Douglas fir for an authentic Snohomish County craftsman look.
— Floating mantel shelves in walnut, reclaimed wood, or painted wood. Minimal trim for a clean, contemporary look.
— Reclaimed barn wood or hand-hewn timber mantels with natural character, knots, and texture.
We also build full fireplace surrounds using wood paneling, stone veneer, tile, or combinations of materials. The surround frames the firebox and creates a visual anchor for the room.

Trim work is the connective tissue of your home's interior design. It includes baseboards, door casings, window casings, chair rail, and any other profiles that frame openings and transitions. Consistent, well-installed trim makes every room feel polished and complete.
We install trim in a range of profiles to match your home's style:
— Rounded profiles with ogee curves, typically 3.25 to 5.25 inches for baseboards and 2.25 to 3.5 inches for casings.
— Flat, square-edged profiles with clean lines. Wide baseboards (5.25 to 7.25 inches) and thick casings create the substantial look characteristic of the style.
— Narrow, flat profiles or shadow-gap details for a minimalist look.

We also install interior doors, including pre-hung doors, slab doors in existing frames, pocket doors, barn doors, and French doors. Door style should complement the trim profile and the overall interior design.

A staircase is one of the most visible architectural features in a two-story home. We build and remodel staircases including new treads and risers, newel posts, balusters, handrails, and landing trim. Options range from traditional wood balusters to modern cable rail, wrought iron, and glass panel systems.

Stair remodeling can dramatically change the feel of an entryway or main living area. Replacing carpeted stairs with hardwood treads and painted risers is one of the most popular finish carpentry projects we perform. We ensure proper tread depth, riser height, and handrail dimensions that meet code requirements while achieving the aesthetic you want.
Beyond the common categories, we build and install a wide range of custom carpentry elements that add character and craftsmanship to your home:
Coffered ceilings and ceiling beams (real wood or decorative hollow beams)
Window seats and bay window framing
Custom cabinet doors and drawer fronts
— We visit your home, discuss your vision, take measurements, and review style and material options.
— We provide a detailed written estimate with material specifications, dimensions, and finish details.
— We source lumber, millwork, and hardware from local suppliers and specialty millwork shops.
— Much of the work is done on-site to ensure precise fits. Larger built-ins may be partially fabricated in a shop and assembled on-site.
— Sanding, filling, caulking, priming, and painting or staining. We leave your home clean and the work ready to enjoy.
The right wood species depends on whether the finished piece will be painted or stained, the level of durability needed, and your budget:
— Smooth, stable, and affordable. The standard choice for painted trim, built-ins, and molding.
— Smooth, consistent, and cost-effective for painted applications. Works well for flat-panel wainscoting and simple trim profiles.
— A Pacific Northwest hardwood with a warm, reddish tone. Popular for stain-grade trim and cabinetry in craftsman and rustic styles.
— Hard, smooth, and light in color. Takes stain and paint well. Good for built-ins and closet systems.
— Durable and versatile with a prominent grain pattern. A premium choice for stain-grade trim, mantels, and built-ins.
— Rich, dark, and striking. A high-end choice for floating mantels, accent shelves, and feature pieces.
— The traditional choice for craftsman homes in the Pacific Northwest. Tight, straight grain with a warm honey tone.
How much does custom carpentry cost in Everett, WA?

Custom carpentry costs vary widely based on the scope and complexity of the project. Crown molding installation typically costs $5 to $15 per linear foot. Built-in bookshelves range from $2,000 to $8,000 depending on size and finish. Custom closet systems range from $3,000 to $10,000. We provide detailed written estimates for every project.
Can you match existing trim and molding in my home?

Yes. Matching existing trim profiles is a common part of our work, especially in remodels and additions. If the original profile is still available from millwork suppliers, we source an exact match. If it has been discontinued, we can have custom profiles milled to match your existing trim precisely.
How long does it take to install built-in shelving?

A standard built-in bookshelf or entertainment center takes 3 to 7 days to build and install on-site, depending on the size, complexity, and finish requirements. Simpler projects like crown molding installation in a single room can be completed in 1 to 2 days.
What types of wood do you use for custom carpentry?

We work with a range of wood species depending on the project and your preferences. Common choices include paint-grade poplar and MDF for painted work, clear-grade alder and maple for stain-grade trim, walnut and white oak for premium built-ins, and reclaimed wood for rustic or character-driven projects. We help you select the right material for the look and budget.
Do you build custom closet systems?

Yes. We design and build custom closet organizer systems tailored to your wardrobe and storage needs. Unlike modular systems from big-box stores, our custom closets are built to fit the exact dimensions of your space, use real wood or high-quality materials, and include features like built-in drawers, shoe racks, pull-out hampers, and jewelry trays.
Tell us about your carpentry project and we will get back to you within one business day.
Ready to Add Custom Details to Your Home?
Call us today for a free consultation on your carpentry project. From crown molding to complete built-ins, we bring craftsmanship to every detail.

text_segments: Custom wood and composite decks designed for the Pacific Northwest. Built to last, built to code, built for how you live outdoors.
Custom Decks Built for the Pacific Northwest

A well-built deck extends your living space outdoors and becomes one of the most-used areas of your home during the warmer months. In the Pacific Northwest, where we enjoy long summer evenings and mild shoulder seasons, a deck is not just an amenity; it is a central part of how families spend time at home. But building a deck in this climate also means building for rain, moisture, and the occasional windstorm. That requires proper materials, engineering, and construction techniques.

NW General Contractor designs and builds custom decks throughout Everett and Snohomish County. Whether you want a low-maintenance composite deck for entertaining, a covered patio for year-round use, or a multi-level cedar deck with built-in seating and lighting, we handle every phase from design through completion.
Wood vs. Composite Decking: Making the Right Choice

The most important decision in any deck project is the decking material. Each option has distinct advantages, and the right choice depends on your budget, maintenance preferences, and aesthetic goals.

Composite decking is made from a blend of wood fibers and plastic polymers, creating a material that resists moisture, rot, insects, and UV fading. It is the most popular choice among our Everett clients for good reason:
— No staining, sealing, or painting required. Occasional cleaning with soap and water is all that is needed.
— Composite boards do not absorb water, which means no swelling, warping, or splitting in the wet PNW climate.
— Premium composite products carry 25-year or lifetime warranties against structural defects and fading.

— Modern composite decking closely mimics the look of natural wood, with realistic grain patterns and color variation. Brands like Trex Transcend, TimberTech Advanced PVC, and Fiberon Concordia offer premium aesthetics.
— Composite comes in a wide range of colors, from traditional wood tones to grays and darker shades that suit modern home designs.

The primary trade-off is cost. Composite decking material costs more than wood, typically $8 to $14 per square foot for the boards alone, compared to $3 to $6 for pressure-treated lumber. However, when you factor in the cost of staining and maintaining a wood deck over 10 to 15 years, composite often breaks even or comes out ahead.

is a traditional PNW decking choice. It is naturally resistant to rot and insects, has a warm reddish-brown color, and is lighter in weight than pressure-treated lumber. Cedar requires annual or biannual cleaning and sealing to maintain its appearance and longevity. Left untreated, it will weather to a silver-gray over time.

is the most affordable decking option. It is southern pine that has been chemically treated to resist rot and insect damage. Pressure-treated decks need to be stained and sealed after an initial drying period and maintained every 1 to 2 years. It is a practical choice for homeowners who prefer a lower upfront cost and do not mind the regular maintenance.
Beyond the decking surface itself, we build a range of features that enhance the function and appearance of your outdoor space:

— A solid roof structure over part or all of the deck allows year-round use, even during the rainy months. We build patio covers with exposed beams, tongue-and-groove ceilings, and integrated gutters for a clean, finished look.
— An open-beam structure that provides partial shade and defines the outdoor space. Pergolas work well with climbing plants and can be fitted with retractable shade fabric or louvered panels.

— Aluminum, cable, glass panel, composite, and traditional wood railings. Railing style has a major impact on the deck's appearance and views. Cable railings and glass panels maintain sightlines while meeting code requirements.
— For sloped lots or elevated decks, we build stairs with proper rise and run, code-compliant handrails, and landings. Multi-level decks create distinct zones for dining, lounging, and cooking.
— Integrated benches along the perimeter, planter boxes at corners, and storage benches that double as seating.

— Low-voltage LED post caps, stair lights, under-rail lighting, and recessed deck lights. Outdoor lighting extends the usability of your deck into the evening and adds safety on stairs and transitions.
— Built-in grill surrounds, countertop space, storage, and utility connections for gas and water.
Deck construction costs depend on the materials, size, height, and complexity of the design. Here are the typical ranges for projects in Snohomish County:
Covered patio or deck with roof (add-on)

These prices include footings, framing (pressure-treated substructure regardless of decking material), decking, railings, stairs, and labor. Covered structures, built-in features, and premium railing systems add to the cost. We provide a detailed, itemized estimate so you know exactly what is included before construction begins.

Everett receives approximately 37 inches of rain per year, and the surrounding Snohomish County area sees even more in higher elevations. Building a deck that will hold up in this climate requires specific construction practices:

— The ledger board connects the deck to the house and is the most common failure point in deck construction. We use through-bolts or structural screws with proper flashing to create a waterproof connection that prevents rot at the house wall.

— Deck boards must have proper spacing for water drainage. The area beneath the deck needs adequate airflow to prevent moisture buildup. We also install ground cover fabric to suppress vegetation growth under the deck.

— Footings in Snohomish County must extend below the frost line (typically 12 inches) and be sized appropriately for the load they carry. We use concrete pier footings with post bases that keep the posts above the concrete to prevent moisture wicking.
Hot-dipped galvanized or stainless steel hardware

— All joist hangers, post bases, bolts, and screws must be rated for ground contact and moisture exposure. We use Simpson Strong-Tie hardware throughout, with hot-dipped galvanized or stainless steel fasteners that will not corrode in the wet climate.
— Regardless of the decking material (composite, cedar, or PT), the structural framing beneath the deck is always pressure-treated lumber rated for ground contact where applicable.
Permits for Deck Building in Everett

Most decks in Everett and Snohomish County require a building permit. A permit is generally required when the deck is more than 30 inches above grade at any point, when it is attached to the house, or when it includes a roof or cover structure. The permit process includes plan submittal, review, and inspections at the footing and framing stages.

Ground-level decks (less than 30 inches above grade and freestanding) may be exempt from permits in some jurisdictions, but we recommend confirming with the local building department before starting work. We handle all permit applications and inspections as part of our service.
— We visit your property, discuss your vision, review the site conditions, and talk through material options and budget.
— We create a deck plan with dimensions, material specifications, and a detailed written estimate.
— We submit the permit application and handle plan review and any revisions.

Most deck projects in Everett take 1 to 3 weeks for construction. A straightforward ground-level deck can often be completed in 5 to 7 working days. Larger decks with multiple levels, stairs, and covered sections take 2 to 3 weeks. Covered patios with roofing can add another week. Permit processing typically takes 2 to 4 weeks before construction begins.
How much does it cost to build a deck in Everett, WA?

Deck construction in Everett typically costs between $15,000 and $30,000 for a standard-sized deck (200-400 square feet). Pressure-treated wood decks are at the lower end, while composite decks with premium railings and built-in features are at the higher end. Covered decks and multi-level designs can exceed $30,000 depending on scope.
Should I choose wood or composite decking?

In the Pacific Northwest, composite decking (Trex, TimberTech) is the most popular choice because it resists moisture, does not rot, and requires virtually no maintenance. Wood decks (cedar or pressure-treated) cost less upfront but require annual cleaning and periodic staining or sealing to withstand the wet climate. We help you weigh the upfront cost versus long-term maintenance when making your decision.
Do I need a permit to build a deck in Everett?

Most decks in Everett require a building permit, especially if the deck is more than 30 inches above grade, is attached to the house, or includes a roof structure. The permit process includes plan review and inspections of footings, framing, and the completed deck. We handle all permit requirements as part of our service.
How long does it take to build a deck?

A larger elevated deck with stairs, railings, and a cover may take 2 to 3 weeks. Permit processing adds 2 to 4 weeks before construction begins.
How do I protect my deck from Pacific Northwest weather?

For wood decks, annual cleaning and resealing or staining is essential to prevent moisture damage, mildew, and UV fading. For composite decks, occasional cleaning with soap and water is usually sufficient. We also recommend proper ventilation beneath the deck, adequate slope for drainage, and flashing at the ledger board connection to prevent water intrusion.
